subject: Physics
title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
summary: The second half of electrostatics: potential and potential energy, the dipole and a system of charges, equipotential surfaces, what a conductor and a dielectric do inside a field, and the capacitor with its combinations and stored energy. With Chapter 1 it forms Unit I, and its derivations and capacitor numericals appear in almost every board paper.

exam_profile.weightage: Unit I (Electrostatics: Chapters 1 and 2) and Unit II (Current Electricity) together carry 16 marks in the CBSE Class 12 Physics paper. This chapter typically contributes about 6 to 8 marks: one 5-mark derivation (dipole potential or the parallel plate capacitor with a dielectric) or a 3-mark capacitor numerical, plus one or two 1-mark questions.

question_types.note: Potential at the centre of a charged shell, potential on the equatorial line of a dipole, shape of equipotential surfaces, work done on an equipotential surface, what changes when a dielectric is inserted or the plates are pulled apart, energy density, and energy lost when a charged capacitor shares its charge.
Field perpendicular to an equipotential surface, potential constant inside a conductor, capacitance independent of the charge given, and energy change when a dielectric is inserted.

Why potential is constant inside a conductor; why two equipotential surfaces cannot cross; sketch equipotential surfaces for a point charge, a uniform field or a dipole; series-to-parallel ratio of three identical capacitors; energy ratio when a charged capacitor is connected to an uncharged one; E and V graphs against r.

Potential energy of a dipole from a given torque; unknown C and V from a change of charge; charge on each capacitor in a series-parallel network; the point where the potential of two charges is zero; work to dissociate three charges; energy before and after a dielectric with the battery connected or removed.

Derivations: potential due to a dipole (axial, equatorial, general point); parallel plate capacitance with and without a dielectric slab; energy density (energy stored, U = Q<sup>2</sup>/2C, is formula-only in the current CBSE syllabus, not a derivation); potential energy of two charges in an external field; each usually paired with a numerical.
A passage on dielectrics in a capacitor, or on equipotential surfaces and potential, followed by four one-line or one-step parts.

hot_topics: Potential due to an electric dipole at a general point, with the axial and equatorial special cases
Parallel plate capacitor: C = ε<sub>0</sub>A/d, and the capacitance with a dielectric slab fully or partly filling the gap
What changes (Q, V, E, C, U) when a dielectric is inserted or the plates are separated, with the battery connected versus disconnected
Series and parallel combinations: equivalent capacitance, charge on each capacitor, energy stored
Energy stored in a capacitor, energy density, and the energy lost when two capacitors share charge
Equipotential surfaces: properties, standard sketches, and the relation E = −dV/dr
Potential energy of a system of charges and of a dipole in a uniform field
Electrostatics of conductors: field zero inside, potential constant, charge on the surface, shielding

sections.heading: 2.1 Introduction
sections.body:
Chapter 1 described the electric field by the force it exerts. This chapter describes the same field by the work it does. The electrostatic force is conservative: the work done in taking a charge from one point to another does not depend on the path, and the work done around any closed path is zero. That is exactly the property that lets us define a potential energy, just as we do for gravity.

Everything in the chapter grows from that one fact. Potential energy per unit charge is the electrostatic potential, a scalar, and it is far easier to add scalars from many charges than to add field vectors. Surfaces of constant potential give a picture of the field. The potential of a conductor is constant, and that leads to the capacitor, a device that stores charge and energy, and to the effect of a dielectric between its plates.

For the exam the chapter is a set of derivations to be written in full (dipole potential, parallel plate capacitance, energy density, series and parallel combinations) plus numericals on capacitor networks and on what changes when a dielectric goes in. One thing to note before you start: the current CBSE syllabus asks for the energy-stored-in-a-capacitor result, U = Q2/2C = ½CV2 = ½QV, as a formula only — its derivation is not examined, even though it is shown in full in Section 2.15 for understanding. Both the derivations and the numericals are covered section by section below.
sections.tip: Everywhere in this chapter the work done by the external agent is minus the work done by the field. Keep that sign straight and half the conceptual questions answer themselves.

sections.heading: 2.2 Electrostatic Potential
sections.body:
Take a fixed charge configuration and bring a test charge q from a point R to a point P slowly, so that it gains no kinetic energy. The external force just balances the electric force, and the work it does, WRP, is stored as the increase of potential energy UP − UR. Because the force is conservative, this work is the same along every path from R to P. Only differences of potential energy are physically meaningful, so we choose a zero: the potential energy is taken as zero at infinity.

Since the work done is proportional to q, we divide it out. Electrostatic potential V at a point is the work done by an external force in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point, without acceleration. Potential difference between two points is the work done per unit positive charge in taking it from one point to the other: VP − VR = WRP/q. The SI unit is the volt, 1 V = 1 J C−1. Potential is a scalar and can be positive, negative or zero. Its dimensional formula is [ML2T−3A−1].

In the exam write the definition with the three qualifying phrases: unit positive charge, from infinity, without acceleration. A question that says the work done by the field is W means the potential energy has fallen by W, so watch which agent the question is talking about.

where: work done by the external force in taking q from R to P without acceleration (J)
work done in bringing q from infinity to P

sections.tip: Potential is defined per unit positive charge; the value at a point does not depend on the test charge you use to measure it.

sections.heading: 2.3 Potential due to a Point Charge
sections.body:
This is the first derivation of the chapter and it is short enough to be asked for 2 marks. Place a charge Q at the origin. The field at a distance r' from it is E = Q/(4πε0r'2), directed radially outward for positive Q. Bring a unit positive test charge from infinity to the point P at distance r. At each step the external force is equal and opposite to the electric force, so the work done by the external force in a small displacement Δr' (towards Q) is ΔW = −E Δr'.

W = −∫∞r (Q/4πε0r'2) dr' = (Q/4πε0) [1/r']∞r = Q/(4πε0r).

By definition this work is the potential: V(r) = Q/(4πε0r). It is positive for positive Q, negative for negative Q, and it falls as 1/r while the field falls as 1/r2. The graph of V against r is a rectangular hyperbola starting high near the charge; the E graph lies below it and drops faster. Both are asked as a 2-mark sketch.

Two checks the examiner likes. First, the potential of a positive charge is positive everywhere, because you have to do work against repulsion to bring a positive test charge in. Second, the potential depends only on r, so all points at the same distance from Q have the same potential; that is the equipotential sphere of section 2.6.

where: distance of the point from the charge (m)

sections.tip: Unlike the field formula, this one takes the sign of Q. For a negative charge V is negative; do not report a magnitude.

sections.heading: 2.4 Potential due to an Electric Dipole
sections.body:
A dipole has charges −q and +q separated by 2a, dipole moment p = q × 2a along the axis from −q to +q. Take the centre O as origin and a point P at distance r from O, the line OP making angle θ with the axis. Let r1 be the distance of P from +q and r2 its distance from −q. Potential is a scalar, so

V = (q/4πε0) (1/r1 − 1/r2).

From the geometry, r12 = r2 + a2 − 2ar cos θ and r22 = r2 + a2 + 2ar cos θ. For a point far from the dipole (r ≫ a), drop a2/r2 and use the binomial approximation: 1/r1 ≈ (1/r)(1 + a cos θ/r) and 1/r2 ≈ (1/r)(1 − a cos θ/r). Subtracting, 1/r1 − 1/r2 ≈ 2a cos θ/r2, so

V = (1/4πε0) · q · 2a cos θ/r2 = (1/4πε0) · p cos θ/r2 = (1/4πε0) · p·r̂/r2.

Special cases the marking scheme expects: on the axis (θ = 0° or 180°) V = ±p/(4πε0r2), positive on the side of +q; on the equatorial plane (θ = 90°) V = 0 everywhere. Without the approximation, the axial potential is V = p/(4πε0(r2 − a2)). Two contrasts with a single charge close the answer: the dipole potential falls as 1/r2, not 1/r, and it depends on the angle θ, not only on r. Because the equatorial plane is at zero potential, no work is done in moving a charge anywhere on it, a favourite 1-mark question.

where: angle between the dipole axis and the line from the centre to the point
distance of the point from the centre of the dipole
on the side of the positive charge

sections.tip: Write the two distances, the two approximations and the final vector form p·r̂/r<sup>2</sup>; each is a marking point. Then state the axial and equatorial results explicitly.

sections.heading: 2.5 Potential due to a System of Charges
sections.body:
For charges q1, q2, ..., qn at distances r1P, r2P, ..., rnP from a point P, the superposition principle gives the potential as the algebraic (scalar) sum:

V = (1/4πε0) (q1/r1P + q2/r2P + ... + qn/rnP).

Signs of the charges go in; no components, no angles. This is why potential is so convenient: the potential at the centre of a hexagon with six equal charges at its vertices is simply six times the potential of one (NCERT 2.2), whereas the field there is zero by symmetry. For a continuous distribution the sum becomes an integral over charge elements.

A uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius R and charge q is the standard example. Outside the shell (r ≥ R) the field is that of a point charge at the centre, so V = q/(4πε0r). Inside (r < R) the field is zero, so no work is done in moving a charge about and the potential is constant, equal to its value on the surface: V = q/(4πε0R). This is why a hollow metal sphere charged to 10 V on its surface is at 10 V at its centre too. The V–r graph is flat inside the sphere and falls as 1/r outside; the E–r graph is zero inside, jumps to σ/ε0 at the surface and falls as 1/r2.

The point where the net potential of two charges is zero is a regular 2- or 3-mark numerical. Set q1/x = |q2|/(d − x) for the point between them and q1/x = |q2|/(x − d) for the point beyond the smaller charge; there are two such points when the charges are of opposite sign.

where: the i-th charge with its sign
distance of q<sub>i</sub> from the point P

formulas.expr: Shell: V = q/(4πε<sub>0</sub>r) for r ≥ R;  V = q/(4πε<sub>0</sub>R) for r < R

sections.tip: Zero field at a point does not mean zero potential there, and zero potential does not mean zero field. The centre of the hexagon and the equatorial plane of a dipole are the two examples to quote.

sections.heading: 2.6 Equipotential Surfaces and the Relation between Field and Potential
sections.body:
An equipotential surface is a surface on which the potential has the same value at every point. For a single point charge the surfaces are concentric spheres centred on the charge; for a uniform field they are planes perpendicular to the field; for a dipole they are the closed curves around each charge, with the equatorial plane as the zero-potential surface; for two equal positive charges they are peanut-shaped surfaces that surround both charges at large distances.

Properties, each worth a mark when asked:

  • No work is done in moving a charge on an equipotential surface, because the potential difference between any two points on it is zero.
  • The electric field is always normal to the equipotential surface. If it had a tangential component, work would be done in moving a charge along the surface, contradicting the first point.
  • Two equipotential surfaces can never intersect. At the crossing the potential would have two values, and the field would have two directions.
  • The surfaces are crowded where the field is strong and spread out where it is weak. Around a point charge, equal steps of potential need larger and larger steps in r, so the spheres are not equally spaced.

Relation between E and V. Take two close equipotential surfaces at V and V + δV, separated by a perpendicular distance δl. The work done by the field in moving a unit positive charge from the first to the second is |E| δl. It also equals the drop in potential, −δV. So |E| δl = −δV, that is

E = −δV/δl.

Two conclusions the examiner wants stated: the field points in the direction in which the potential decreases most steeply, and its magnitude is the rate of change of potential with distance along that direction, the potential gradient, in V m−1 (identical to N C−1).

where: potential gradient along the normal to the equipotential surface (V m<sup>−1</sup>)
the field points towards decreasing potential
work done in moving any charge between two points of the surface

sections.tip: When asked to draw equipotential surfaces for a uniform field, draw equally spaced parallel planes; for a field that increases along z, draw planes that get closer together as z increases.

sections.heading: 2.7 Potential Energy of a System of Charges
sections.body:
The potential energy of a system of charges is the work done in assembling it, bringing the charges from infinity to their positions. Start with two charges. Bring q1 first: no field exists yet, so no work is done. Now bring q2 to a point at distance r12 from q1. The work done is q2 times the potential of q1 at that point:

U = W = q2V1 = (1/4πε0) · q1q2/r12.

The result is symmetric in the two charges, so the order of assembly does not matter, and because the force is conservative the path does not matter either. Like charges give positive U (work must be done to push them together), unlike charges negative U (the field does the work).

For three charges, bring q3 last. It moves in the field of both earlier charges, so the extra work is q3(V1 + V2) and

U = (1/4πε0) (q1q2/r12 + q1q3/r13 + q2q3/r23).

In general the potential energy is the sum over every pair of charges, each pair counted once. The work required to dissociate a system, that is to separate the charges to infinity, is −U. For three charges 1 μC, 1 μC and −4 μC at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 10 cm, U = 9 × 109 × 10−12 × (1 − 4 − 4)/0.1 = −0.63 J, so 0.63 J of work is needed to pull the system apart; that exact numerical has been set in the board paper.

where: each pair of charges counted exactly once

sections.tip: For four charges there are six pairs, not four. Count the diagonals of a square, and remember a diagonal is √2 times the side.

sections.heading: 2.8 Potential Energy in an External Field
sections.body:
Now the field is produced by sources outside the system and is not changed by the charges we bring in. Single charge. The potential energy of q at a point where the external potential is V(r) is U = qV(r), the work done in bringing q from infinity to that point. One electron-volt is the energy gained by an electron accelerated through 1 V: 1 eV = 1.6 × 10−19 J.

Two charges. Bring q1 to r1: work q1V(r1). Bring q2 to r2: it works against the external field and against the field of q1, so the work is q2V(r2) + q1q2/(4πε0r12). The total is

U = q1V(r1) + q2V(r2) + q1q2/(4πε0r12).

Dipole in a uniform field (the derivation most often asked from this section). A dipole of moment p at angle θ to a uniform field E experiences a torque τ = pE sin θ and no net force. To rotate it slowly from θ0 to θ1 an external torque does work

W = ∫θ0θ1 pE sin θ dθ = pE(cos θ0 − cos θ1),

which is the change in potential energy U(θ1) − U(θ0). Choose the zero at θ0 = 90°, the position where the dipole is perpendicular to the field. Then

U(θ) = −pE cos θ = −p·E.

U is least (−pE) at θ = 0°, the stable equilibrium, and greatest (+pE) at θ = 180°, the unstable equilibrium. The work needed to turn the dipole from the aligned position through 180° is 2pE. A typical 3-mark question gives the torque and the angle, asks you to find pE from τ = pE sin θ, and then U = −pE cos θ.

where: external potential at the position of q

formulas.expr: U(θ) = −pE cos θ = −p·E; W = pE(cos θ0 − cos θ1)
where: work done by the external agent in turning the dipole from θ<sub>0</sub> to θ<sub>1</sub>

sections.tip: State that the zero of U is taken at θ = 90° before writing U = −pE cos θ; the marking scheme rewards it. The torque is zero at both 0° and 180°, but only 0° is stable.

sections.heading: 2.9 Electrostatics of Conductors
sections.body:
A conductor has free electrons that move until, in the static situation, there is no force on them. Every result below follows from that, and NCERT lists six. Learn them as numbered statements with the one-line reason each.

  1. The electrostatic field is zero inside a conductor. If it were not, free charges would move, and the situation would not be static. This holds whether the conductor is neutral or charged, and in an external field.
  2. At the surface, the field is normal to the surface at every point. A tangential component would drive surface charges along the surface. For a charged conductor the field just outside is E = (σ/ε0) n̂, obtained by Gauss's law on a small pill-box straddling the surface with one face inside where E = 0.
  3. In the static situation there is no excess charge inside the conductor. Gauss's law on any surface inside gives zero flux, so zero enclosed charge; any excess charge sits on the surface.
  4. The potential is constant throughout the volume and has the same value on the surface. With E = 0 inside and no tangential field on the surface, no work is done in moving a test charge between any two points, so the potential difference is zero. This is the 2-mark question that appears again and again.
  5. Surface charge density σ may vary from point to point, larger where the surface is sharply curved, but E = σ/ε0 locally.
  6. Electrostatic shielding. The field inside a cavity of a conductor is zero whatever the charges or fields outside. A sensitive instrument is protected by enclosing it in a metal box; sitting inside a car during lightning is safer for the same reason.

A conductor is therefore an equipotential volume. Two conductors at different potentials joined by a wire exchange charge until they reach a common potential; for two spheres that means Q1/R1 = Q2/R2, so the smaller sphere carries the higher surface charge density.

where: outward unit normal to the surface
the same inside the body, on its surface and in any cavity

sections.tip: For the 2-mark 'why is the potential constant inside a conductor' question, the answer is the argument, not the fact: E = 0 inside, so no work is done moving a charge, so no potential difference.

sections.heading: 2.10 Dielectrics and Polarisation
sections.body:
A dielectric is an insulator with no free charges. Placed in an external field, it does not cancel the field the way a conductor does, but it does reduce it. The mechanism depends on the kind of molecule.

Non-polar molecules (H2, O2, N2, CO2) have the centres of positive and negative charge coinciding and no permanent dipole moment. An external field pulls the two centres apart, giving each molecule an induced dipole moment in the direction of the field. Polar molecules (HCl, H2O) have a permanent dipole moment, but thermal motion keeps the moments randomly oriented so the net moment is zero. An external field partly aligns them, more strongly at low temperature.

In both cases the dielectric acquires a net dipole moment along the field: it is polarised. The polarisation P is the dipole moment per unit volume, and for a linear isotropic dielectric P = χeE, where χe is the electric susceptibility. Inside the material the aligned dipoles cancel in the bulk, but on the two faces perpendicular to the field appear layers of uncoupled charge, the induced surface charge density ±σp. These layers produce a field opposite to the external one, so the net field inside the dielectric is smaller than the applied field: E = E0/K, where K is the dielectric constant.

This is the answer to the 1-mark classic: a plastic sheet between two charged balls reduces the force between them because the sheet becomes polarised and its induced charges weaken the field. Every dielectric has a dielectric strength, the maximum field it can stand before it breaks down and conducts; for air it is about 3 × 106 V m−1, which sets the maximum charge a capacitor can hold.

where: polarisation, dipole moment per unit volume (C m<sup>−2</sup>)
field that would exist in vacuum

sections.tip: Distinguish a dielectric from a conductor in one line: a conductor reduces the internal field to zero by moving free charges; a dielectric only reduces it, by polarisation of bound charges.

sections.heading: 2.11 Capacitors and Capacitance
sections.body:
A capacitor is a pair of conductors separated by an insulator, carrying charges +Q and −Q. Q is called the charge of the capacitor, and V is the potential difference between the conductors. The field in the gap is proportional to Q, so V is proportional to Q, and the ratio

C = Q/V

is the capacitance. It measures how much charge the capacitor holds per volt of potential difference. C depends only on the geometry of the conductors (size, shape, separation) and on the medium between them; it does not depend on Q or V. The SI unit is the farad, 1 F = 1 C V−1. A farad is enormous, so practical values are in microfarads (1 μF = 10−6 F), nanofarads and picofarads (1 pF = 10−12 F). The dimensional formula is [M−1L−2T4A2].

A single isolated conductor is also a capacitor, with the second conductor at infinity. An isolated sphere of radius R has V = Q/(4πε0R), so C = 4πε0R, proportional to the radius.

The charge a capacitor can hold is limited by the dielectric strength of the medium. For a given C, a large charge means a large V and hence a large field, and once the field exceeds the dielectric strength the insulation breaks down and charge leaks across. That is why high-voltage capacitors need thick or strong insulation. On a circuit diagram a capacitor is two equal parallel lines; a variable capacitor has an arrow across them.

The 3-mark numerical from this section: a capacitor charged to V holds 360 μC; reducing V by 120 V leaves 120 μC. Then C(V − 120) = 120 and CV = 360 give C = 2 μF, V = 180 V, and at 300 V the charge is 600 μC.

where: radius of an isolated conducting sphere

sections.tip: If a question says the charge is doubled and asks for the new capacitance, the answer is 'unchanged'. Capacitance is a property of the device, not of its state.

sections.heading: 2.12 The Parallel Plate Capacitor
sections.body:
Two large plane parallel conducting plates, each of area A, are separated by a small distance d (d much smaller than the plate dimensions, so edge effects can be ignored). Plate 1 carries +Q and plate 2 carries −Q, so the surface charge densities are σ = Q/A and −σ.

Each plate produces a field σ/2ε0 on both sides, directed away from the positive plate and towards the negative one (Gauss's law for an infinite plane sheet, Chapter 1). Outside the capacitor the two fields are opposite and cancel: E = σ/2ε0 − σ/2ε0 = 0. Between the plates they add:

E = σ/2ε0 + σ/2ε0 = σ/ε0 = Q/(ε0A),

uniform and directed from the positive plate to the negative plate. For a uniform field the potential difference is field times separation:

V = Ed = Qd/(ε0A).

Therefore C = Q/V = ε0A/d.

The result carries the two expected features: C grows with plate area and falls as the plates are separated, and it depends only on geometry. Numerically, ε0 = 8.85 × 10−12 F m−1, so plates of 1 m2 separated by 1 mm give only 8.85 nF; that is why a farad is so large. For NCERT 2.8, A = 6 × 10−3 m2 and d = 3 mm give C = 17.7 pF.

In the exam draw the two plates with +σ and −σ, mark the field lines only between the plates, and state E = 0 outside before writing V = Ed. Questions that halve d, or double A, or do both, are direct substitutions into this formula, but read carefully whether the battery stays connected (V fixed) or is removed (Q fixed) before you say what happens to the charge or the potential.
sections.tip: Write 'E = 0 outside the plates because the fields of the two sheets cancel' as a separate line; it is a marking point that students skip.

sections.heading: 2.13 Effect of Dielectric on Capacitance
sections.body:
Fill the gap of a parallel plate capacitor with a dielectric slab. The plates carry ±σ as before. The dielectric is polarised and its faces next to the plates acquire induced charge densities −σp (next to the positive plate) and +σp. The net field inside the dielectric is due to σ − σp:

E = (σ − σp)/ε0.

For a linear dielectric σp is proportional to σ, so we write σ − σp = σ/K, where K > 1 is the dielectric constant. Then E = σ/(ε0K) = E0/K, the potential difference is V = Ed = σd/(ε0K) = Qd/(Kε0A), and

C = Q/V = Kε0A/d = K C0.

The capacitance increases K times. The product ε = Kε0 is the permittivity of the medium and K = ε/ε0 = εr is its relative permittivity; K is also C/C0, the ratio of the capacitance with the dielectric to that without.

Slab of thickness t < d (the 5-mark version). The field is E0 = σ/ε0 in the air gap of total thickness d − t and E0/K inside the slab of thickness t. So V = E0(d − t) + (E0/K)t = (σ/ε0)(d − t + t/K), and

C = ε0A/(d − t + t/K).

Put t = d and this returns Kε0A/d; put K → ∞ (a conducting slab) and it gives ε0A/(d − t). A slab of thickness 3d/4 gives C/C0 = 4K/(K + 3).

What changes when a dielectric is inserted. With the battery still connected, V is fixed: C rises to KC0, Q rises to KQ0, E = V/d is unchanged, and U = ½CV2 rises K times. With the battery disconnected first, Q is fixed: C rises to KC0, V falls to V0/K, E falls to E0/K, and U = Q2/2C falls to U0/K. Write these as a two-column table in the answer; it is asked in almost every alternate year in one form or another.

where: capacitance with vacuum (or air) between the plates
thickness of the dielectric slab, t < d

formulas.expr: Battery connected: V same, Q → KQ, U → KU.  Battery removed: Q same, V → V/K, E → E/K, U → U/K

sections.tip: Before answering any 'dielectric inserted' question, write down which quantity is held fixed: V if the battery is connected, Q if it has been removed. Every other change follows from Q = CV.

sections.heading: 2.14 Combination of Capacitors
sections.body:
Series. Capacitors C1 and C2 are joined end to end and the free ends are connected across V. The battery puts +Q on the first plate of C1; induction puts −Q on its other plate and hence +Q on the first plate of C2, and so on. Every capacitor in series carries the same charge Q. The potential differences add: V = V1 + V2 = Q/C1 + Q/C2. Defining the equivalent capacitance by V = Q/C,

1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2, and in general 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + ... + 1/Cn.

The equivalent capacitance is smaller than the smallest capacitor; n identical capacitors C in series give C/n. The larger the capacitor, the smaller its share of the voltage.

Parallel. Capacitors are connected between the same two points, so each has the same potential difference V. The charges add: Q = Q1 + Q2 = C1V + C2V, so with Q = CV,

C = C1 + C2 + ... + Cn.

n identical capacitors in parallel give nC, so three identical capacitors have a series-to-parallel ratio of 1 : 9, the source of the 'net series capacitance is 1 pF, find the parallel value' question (answer 9 pF, and the energies across the same source are in the same ratio 1 : 9).

Networks. Reduce step by step: series groups first, then parallel, redrawing each time. Then work back outwards: the charge on a series group is the group's equivalent capacitance times the voltage across it, and that charge sits on every member of the group; the voltage across a parallel group is shared by every member. For the standard network of C1, C2, C3 in series and that chain in parallel with C4, all 10 μF across 500 V: the chain is 10/3 μF, the total is 40/3 ≈ 13.3 μF, each of C1, C2, C3 holds (10/3 μF)(500 V) = 1.67 × 10−3 C and C4 holds 5 × 10−3 C.

formulas.expr: Series: 1/C = 1/C<sub>1</sub> + 1/C<sub>2</sub> + ... ;  same Q on each, V = V<sub>1</sub> + V<sub>2</sub> + ...
where: equivalent capacitance, less than the smallest C<sub>i</sub>

formulas.expr: Parallel: C = C<sub>1</sub> + C<sub>2</sub> + ... ;  same V on each, Q = Q<sub>1</sub> + Q<sub>2</sub> + ...
where: equivalent capacitance, more than the largest C<sub>i</sub>

formulas.expr: Two in series: C = C<sub>1</sub>C<sub>2</sub>/(C<sub>1</sub> + C<sub>2</sub>)
where: product over sum; only for exactly two capacitors

sections.tip: Capacitors add the opposite way to resistors: series is the reciprocal rule, parallel is the plain sum. Students who mix them up lose the whole numerical.

sections.heading: 2.15 Energy Stored in a Capacitor
sections.body:
Charging a capacitor means moving charge from one plate to the other against the potential difference that already exists, and the work done is stored as electrostatic energy. Suppose at some stage the plates carry ±Q' so that the potential difference is V' = Q'/C. Moving a further charge δQ' from the negative to the positive plate needs work δW = V' δQ' = (Q'/C) δQ'. Adding all such steps from 0 to the final charge Q:

W = ∫0Q (Q'/C) dQ' = Q2/2C.

So U = Q2/2C = ½CV2 = ½QV. Use the form that keeps the fixed quantity: Q2/2C when the battery has been removed, ½CV2 when it stays connected. Graphically, on a plot of V against Q the area under the straight line is the energy. The current CBSE syllabus lists this topic as 'formulae only, no derivation', so the integral above will not be asked for in the exam — but working through it once is what makes the three equivalent forms of U easy to recall under pressure, which is why it is shown in full here.

Where the energy is. It resides in the field between the plates. For a parallel plate capacitor U = ½CV2 = ½(ε0A/d)(Ed)2 = ½ε0E2 × (Ad). Dividing by the volume Ad gives the energy density

u = ½ε0E2 (J m−3),

a result that holds for any electric field in vacuum; in a dielectric it becomes ½Kε0E2.

Sharing charge. A capacitor C1 charged to V1 is connected to C2 at V2. Charge flows until both reach the common potential V = (C1V1 + C2V2)/(C1 + C2). The total charge is conserved but energy is not: the loss C1C2(V1 − V2)2/2(C1 + C2) is dissipated as heat in the connecting wires and as electromagnetic radiation. In the special case of an uncharged identical capacitor, V becomes V1/2, the energy of the combination is half the initial energy, so exactly half is lost (NCERT 2.11: 600 pF at 200 V loses 6 × 10−6 J). That 1 : 2 ratio is a standing 2-mark question.

where: energy per unit volume of the field (J m<sup>−3</sup>)
energy lost as heat and radiation when the two are connected

sections.tip: When asked why energy is lost on connecting two capacitors, do not say 'energy is not conserved'. Say charge is conserved and the difference in energy is dissipated as heat and radiation in the connecting wires.

key_terms.definition: Work done by an external force in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to a point, without acceleration. Scalar; SI unit volt (J C<sup>−1</sup>).
Work done per unit positive charge in taking it from one point to another: V<sub>P</sub> − V<sub>R</sub> = W<sub>RP</sub>/q. Only differences are physically meaningful.
p = q × 2a for charges ±q separated by 2a, a vector from −q to +q; unit C m. Its potential falls as 1/r<sup>2</sup> and is zero on the equatorial plane.
A surface on which the potential is the same at every point. The field is normal to it, no work is done moving a charge on it, and two such surfaces never intersect.
Rate of change of potential with distance, dV/dr. The field equals minus the potential gradient, E = −dV/dr, and points towards decreasing potential.

key_terms.term: Potential energy of a system of charges
key_terms.definition: Work done in assembling the charges from infinity; the sum of q<sub>i</sub>q<sub>j</sub>/(4πε<sub>0</sub>r<sub>ij</sub>) over every pair of charges, each pair counted once.
The field inside a cavity in a conductor is zero whatever the external field or charges, so a metal enclosure protects whatever is inside it.
An insulator with no free charges which, in an external field, becomes polarised and reduces the field inside itself by a factor K, but does not cancel it.
A polar molecule (HCl, H<sub>2</sub>O) has a permanent dipole moment; a non-polar one (H<sub>2</sub>, O<sub>2</sub>, CO<sub>2</sub>) has none and acquires an induced moment only in a field.
Dipole moment per unit volume of a dielectric, P = χ<sub>e</sub>E for a linear isotropic material; χ<sub>e</sub> is the electric susceptibility.
Ratio of the permittivity of a medium to that of free space, K = ε/ε<sub>0</sub>; equivalently the factor by which the capacitance rises, C/C<sub>0</sub>, or the field falls, E<sub>0</sub>/E.
The maximum electric field a dielectric can withstand without breaking down and conducting; about 3 × 10<sup>6</sup> V m<sup>−1</sup> for air.
C = Q/V, the charge stored per unit potential difference between the two conductors. Depends only on geometry and medium; SI unit farad (C V<sup>−1</sup>).
Energy stored per unit volume of an electric field, u = ½ε<sub>0</sub>E<sup>2</sup> in vacuum, ½Kε<sub>0</sub>E<sup>2</sup> in a dielectric.
The potential two connected capacitors settle at, (C<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> + C<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>)/(C<sub>1</sub> + C<sub>2</sub>); total charge is conserved, some energy is lost.
Energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 1 V; 1 eV = 1.6 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J.

diagrams.title: Equipotential surfaces: point charge, uniform field, dipole, two like charges
diagrams.how_to_draw: Four small sketches. (1) A point charge with three concentric circles, spacing increasing outward, and radial field lines crossing them at right angles. (2) A uniform field as parallel arrows with equally spaced straight lines drawn perpendicular to them. (3) A dipole with closed loops around +q and around −q and a straight line through the centre, the equatorial plane, labelled V = 0. (4) Two equal positive charges with small loops around each merging into one peanut-shaped loop further out. Label each sketch and write 'field lines normal to surfaces' once.

diagrams.title: Geometry for the potential of a dipole
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw −q and +q on a horizontal line with centre O and half-length a on each side; the arrow p points from −q to +q. Mark a point P at distance r from O with angle θ between OP and the axis. Draw lines from +q and −q to P and label them r<sub>1</sub> and r<sub>2</sub>. Beside the figure write V = (q/4πε<sub>0</sub>)(1/r<sub>1</sub> − 1/r<sub>2</sub>) and the final result p cos θ/(4πε<sub>0</sub>r<sup>2</sup>).

diagrams.title: Parallel plate capacitor with a dielectric slab
diagrams.how_to_draw: Two vertical plates labelled +σ and −σ with field lines from left to right between them and none outside. Inside, draw the slab as a rectangle; along its left face write −σ<sub>p</sub> and along its right face +σ<sub>p</sub>. Show the reduced field E = E<sub>0</sub>/K with fewer arrows inside the slab than in any air gap. Mark d, and t if the slab does not fill the gap. Label A for the plate area.

diagrams.title: E and V against r for a point charge and for a charged spherical shell
diagrams.how_to_draw: Two graph pairs. For the point charge, draw V falling as 1/r (a hyperbola) and below it E falling as 1/r<sup>2</sup>, steeper. For the shell of radius R, draw V flat at q/(4πε<sub>0</sub>R) from r = 0 to R and then falling as 1/r; draw E zero from 0 to R, a vertical jump to σ/ε<sub>0</sub> at R, then falling as 1/r<sup>2</sup>. Mark R on both axes.

diagrams.title: Series and parallel combination of capacitors
diagrams.how_to_draw: Series: three capacitors in one line across a battery V; write +Q −Q on each pair of plates to show the same charge, and V<sub>1</sub>, V<sub>2</sub>, V<sub>3</sub> across them. Parallel: three capacitors between the same two rails across V; write Q<sub>1</sub>, Q<sub>2</sub>, Q<sub>3</sub> on them and V across the rails. Under each write the combination rule.

ncert_questions.q: Two charges 5 × 10<sup>−8</sup> C and −3 × 10<sup>−8</sup> C are located 16 cm apart. At what point(s) on the line joining the two charges is the electric potential zero? Take the potential at infinity to be zero.
ncert_questions.a:
Let the point be x cm from the positive charge. Between the charges: (5 × 10−8)/x = (3 × 10−8)/(16 − x) → 5(16 − x) = 3x → 80 = 8x → x = 10 cm.

Beyond the negative charge: 5/x = 3/(x − 16) → 5x − 80 = 3x → x = 40 cm.

The potential is zero at 10 cm from the positive charge (between the charges) and at 40 cm from it on the side of the negative charge. There is no such point on the far side of the positive charge because both distances would favour the larger charge.

ncert_questions.q: A regular hexagon of side 10 cm has a charge 5 μC at each of its vertices. Calculate the potential at the centre of the hexagon.
ncert_questions.a:
Each vertex of a regular hexagon is at a distance equal to the side, 10 cm, from the centre. Potential is a scalar, so the six equal contributions add:

V = 6 × (1/4πε0) q/r = 6 × 9 × 109 × 5 × 10−6/0.10 = 6 × 4.5 × 105 = 2.7 × 106 V.

Note that the field at the centre is zero by symmetry although the potential is not.

ncert_questions.q: Two charges 2 μC and −2 μC are placed at points A and B 6 cm apart. (a) Identify an equipotential surface of the system. (b) What is the direction of the electric field at every point on this surface?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) The plane that bisects AB at right angles (the perpendicular bisector plane) is an equipotential surface at zero potential: every point on it is equidistant from +2 μC and −2 μC, so the two contributions cancel.

(b) The field is normal to the plane at every point, directed from A towards B, that is, from the positive charge to the negative charge along AB.

ncert_questions.q: A spherical conductor of radius 12 cm has a charge of 1.6 × 10<sup>−7</sup> C distributed uniformly on its surface. What is the electric field (a) inside the sphere, (b) just outside the sphere, (c) at a point 18 cm from the centre of the sphere?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Zero. The charge is on the surface and the field inside a charged conductor is zero.

(b) Just outside, E = (1/4πε0) q/R2 = 9 × 109 × 1.6 × 10−7/(0.12)2 = 1440/0.0144 = 1.0 × 105 N C−1, directed radially outward.

(c) At r = 0.18 m, E = 1440/(0.18)2 = 1440/0.0324 = 4.4 × 104 N C−1, radially outward.

ncert_questions.q: A parallel plate capacitor with air between the plates has a capacitance of 8 pF. What will be the capacitance if the distance between the plates is reduced by half and the space between them is filled with a substance of dielectric constant 6?
ncert_questions.a: C = ε0A/d = 8 pF. With d' = d/2 and dielectric K = 6, C' = Kε0A/(d/2) = 2K × (ε0A/d) = 2 × 6 × 8 pF = 96 pF.

ncert_questions.q: Three capacitors each of capacitance 9 pF are connected in series. (a) What is the total capacitance of the combination? (b) What is the potential difference across each capacitor if the combination is connected to a 120 V supply?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) 1/C = 1/9 + 1/9 + 1/9 = 3/9 pF−1, so C = 3 pF.

(b) Charge on the combination Q = CV = 3 × 10−12 × 120 = 3.6 × 10−10 C, the same on each capacitor. Potential difference across each = Q/C1 = 3.6 × 10−10/9 × 10−12 = 40 V. (Identical capacitors in series share the supply equally: 120/3 = 40 V.)

ncert_questions.q: Three capacitors of capacitances 2 pF, 3 pF and 4 pF are connected in parallel. (a) What is the total capacitance of the combination? (b) Determine the charge on each capacitor if the combination is connected to a 100 V supply.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) C = 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 pF.

(b) Each capacitor has 100 V across it. Q1 = 2 × 10−12 × 100 = 2 × 10−10 C; Q2 = 3 × 10−10 C; Q3 = 4 × 10−10 C. Total 9 × 10−10 C = CV, as a check.

ncert_questions.q: In a parallel plate capacitor with air between the plates, each plate has an area of 6 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>2</sup> and the distance between the plates is 3 mm. Calculate the capacitance of the capacitor. If this capacitor is connected to a 100 V supply, what is the charge on each plate of the capacitor?
ncert_questions.a:
C = ε0A/d = 8.85 × 10−12 × 6 × 10−3/3 × 10−3 = 8.85 × 10−12 × 2 = 1.77 × 10−11 F = 17.7 pF.

Q = CV = 1.77 × 10−11 × 100 = 1.77 × 10−9 C on each plate (positive on one, negative on the other).

ncert_questions.q: Explain what would happen if in the capacitor of Exercise 2.8 a 3 mm thick mica sheet (of dielectric constant 6) were inserted between the plates, (a) while the voltage supply remained connected, (b) after the supply was disconnected.
ncert_questions.a:
The mica fills the gap, so in both cases C' = KC = 6 × 17.7 pF = 1.06 × 10−10 F (106 pF).

(a) Supply connected: V stays 100 V. Charge rises to Q' = C'V = 1.06 × 10−10 × 100 = 1.06 × 10−8 C, six times the original.

(b) Supply disconnected: the charge stays Q = 1.77 × 10−9 C. The potential difference falls to V' = Q/C' = 100/6 = 16.7 V, and the field between the plates also falls to one-sixth.

ncert_questions.q: A 12 pF capacitor is connected to a 50 V battery. How much electrostatic energy is stored in the capacitor?
A 600 pF capacitor is charged by a 200 V supply. It is then disconnected from the supply and is connected to another uncharged 600 pF capacitor. How much electrostatic energy is lost in the process?
ncert_questions.a:
Initial energy U1 = ½CV2 = ½ × 600 × 10−12 × (200)2 = 1.2 × 10−5 J.

On connection the charge Q = CV = 1.2 × 10−7 C spreads over the two identical capacitors (total 1200 pF), so the common potential is V' = 1.2 × 10−7/1.2 × 10−9 = 100 V.

Final energy U2 = ½ × 1200 × 10−12 × (100)2 = 6 × 10−6 J.

Energy lost = 1.2 × 10−5 − 6 × 10−6 = 6 × 10−6 J, half the initial energy, dissipated as heat and radiation in the connecting wires.

ncert_questions.q: Four charges are arranged at the corners of a square ABCD of side d: +q at A, −q at B, +q at C, −q at D. (a) Find the work required to put together this arrangement. (b) A charge q<sub>0</sub> is brought to the centre E of the square. How much extra work is needed to do this?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Six pairs. Four adjacent pairs, each of unlike charges at distance d: 4 × (−q2/4πε0d). Two diagonal pairs, each of like charges at distance √2 d: 2 × (q2/4πε0√2 d).

W = U = (q2/4πε0d)(−4 + 2/√2) = −(q2/4πε0d)(4 − √2). The work is negative: the field does the work, and the arrangement has lower energy than four separated charges.

(b) The centre is equidistant from all four charges, and the charges sum to zero, so the potential at E is zero. Extra work = q0 × V(E) = 0.

ncert_questions.q: A 900 pF capacitor is charged by a 100 V battery. (a) How much electrostatic energy is stored by the capacitor? (b) The capacitor is disconnected from the battery and connected to another 900 pF capacitor. What is the electrostatic energy stored by the system?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Q = CV = 900 × 10−12 × 100 = 9 × 10−8 C. U = ½QV = ½ × 9 × 10−8 × 100 = 4.5 × 10−6 J.

(b) The charge divides equally between the two identical capacitors, 4.5 × 10−8 C each, and the potential of each becomes 50 V. Energy of the system = 2 × ½ × 4.5 × 10−8 × 50 = 2.25 × 10−6 J, half the initial energy. The other half is lost as heat and radiation.

pyq.q: A hollow metal sphere of radius 5 cm is charged such that the potential on its surface is 10 V. The potential at the centre of the sphere is
options: same as at a point 5 cm away from the surface
same as at a point 25 cm away from the surface
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The field inside a hollow charged conductor is zero, so no work is done in moving a charge from the surface to the centre. The potential is constant inside and equals the surface value, 10 V.

pyq.q: The electric potential on the axis of an electric dipole at a distance r from its centre is V. Then the potential at a point at the same distance on its equatorial line will be
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: On the equatorial line every point is equidistant from +q and −q, so the two potentials cancel: V = p cos 90°/(4πε<sub>0</sub>r<sup>2</sup>) = 0.

pyq.q: The equipotential surfaces due to a single isolated point charge are
options: parallel planes perpendicular to the field
concentric spherical surfaces centred on the charge
coaxial cylinders with the charge on the axis
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: V = q/(4πε<sub>0</sub>r) depends only on r, so all points at the same distance from the charge are at the same potential: spheres centred on the charge.

pyq.q: A parallel plate capacitor is charged by a battery, which is then disconnected. The separation between the plates is now doubled. Which of the following remains unchanged?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: With the battery removed the plates are isolated, so Q cannot change. C halves (C = ε<sub>0</sub>A/d), V = Q/C doubles, and U = Q<sup>2</sup>/2C doubles.

pyq.q: The work done in moving a charge of 2 μC from a point A at potential 10 V to a point B at potential 30 V is
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: W = q(V<sub>B</sub> − V<sub>A</sub>) = 2 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × (30 − 10) = 4 × 10<sup>−5</sup> J, done by the external agent.

pyq.q: A capacitor of capacitance C is charged to a potential V and then connected to an identical uncharged capacitor. The fraction of the initial energy that is lost is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Charge CV shares between 2C, giving common potential V/2. Final energy ½(2C)(V/2)<sup>2</sup> = ¼CV<sup>2</sup>, half of the initial ½CV<sup>2</sup>.

pyq.q: The energy density in a region of uniform electric field E in vacuum is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: From U = ½CV<sup>2</sup> for a parallel plate capacitor, U/(volume) = ½ε<sub>0</sub>E<sup>2</sup>, and the result holds for any electric field.

pyq.q: A parallel plate capacitor with air between the plates has capacitance C<sub>0</sub>. If the plate separation is doubled and the gap is completely filled with a dielectric of constant K, the new capacitance is
pyq.answer: b

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The electric field at every point on an equipotential surface is perpendicular to the surface. Reason (R): No work is done in moving a charge from one point to another on an equipotential surface.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Because the potential difference on the surface is zero, the work done along it is zero; a tangential field component would do work, so the field must be normal. R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The electrostatic potential at every point inside a hollow charged conductor is zero. Reason (R): The electrostatic field at every point inside a hollow charged conductor is zero.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: The field inside is zero, so the potential is constant, equal to the surface value, not zero. A is false, R is true.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The capacitance of a conductor increases when a larger charge is given to it. Reason (R): Capacitance is defined as C = Q/V.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: V rises in proportion to Q, so their ratio, the capacitance, is fixed by geometry and the medium. A is false; the definition in R is true.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): When a dielectric slab is inserted between the plates of an isolated charged capacitor, the energy stored decreases. Reason (R): The dielectric becomes polarised and the field between the plates is reduced.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: With Q fixed, the polarised dielectric reduces E and hence V, so U = ½QV falls to U/K. R is the physical reason for A.

pyq.q: Why is the electrostatic potential constant throughout the volume of a conductor and has the same value on its surface as inside?
pyq.answer: In the static situation the electric field inside a conductor is zero, and on its surface the field has no tangential component (it is normal to the surface). So no work is done in moving a test charge between any two points inside the conductor or from the inside to the surface. Since potential difference is work per unit charge, the potential difference between any two such points is zero: the potential is constant throughout the volume and equal to its value on the surface.

pyq.q: Can two equipotential surfaces intersect each other? Give reasons. Also, how much work is done in moving a test charge from a point P to a point Q on the equatorial line of an electric dipole?
pyq.answer:
No. If two equipotential surfaces intersected, the point of intersection would have two different values of potential, which is impossible; also the field would have two directions there, since it is normal to each surface.

The equatorial line (plane) of a dipole is at zero potential everywhere, so VP = VQ = 0 and the work done W = q(VQ − VP) = 0.

pyq.q: A capacitor C is charged to a potential difference V and then connected across an identical uncharged capacitor. Find the ratio of the energy stored in the combination to the initial energy stored in the single capacitor.
pyq.answer:
Initial energy U1 = ½CV2. Charge Q = CV is conserved and spreads over 2C, so the common potential is V/2.

Final energy U2 = ½(2C)(V/2)2 = ¼CV2.

U2 : U1 = 1 : 2. Half the energy is lost as heat and radiation in the connecting wires.

pyq.q: Net capacitance of three identical capacitors in series is 1 pF. What will be their net capacitance if connected in parallel? Find the ratio of energy stored in the two configurations if they are both connected to the same source.
pyq.answer:
Series: C/3 = 1 pF, so each capacitor is C = 3 pF. Parallel: 3C = 9 pF.

Across the same source V, U = ½CeqV2, so Useries : Uparallel = 1 : 9.

pyq.q: Draw plots showing the variation of (i) electric field E and (ii) electric potential V with distance r from a point charge Q.
pyq.answer:
(i) E = Q/(4πε0r2): a curve falling steeply as 1/r2, approaching the r-axis but never touching it.

(ii) V = Q/(4πε0r): a rectangular hyperbola falling as 1/r, less steep than the E curve at large r.

Label the axes, mark that both tend to zero as r → ∞, and note that E falls faster than V.

pyq.q: An electric dipole of length 4 cm, when placed with its axis making an angle of 60° with a uniform electric field, experiences a torque of 4√3 N m. Calculate the potential energy of the dipole, if it has charge ±8 nC.

A capacitor of unknown capacitance is charged to a potential V; the charge on it is 360 μC. When the potential across the capacitor is reduced by 120 V, the charge stored becomes 120 μC. Calculate the potential V and the unknown capacitance C. What will be the charge stored in the capacitor if the voltage applied had been increased by 120 V?

Four capacitors C<sub>1</sub>, C<sub>2</sub>, C<sub>3</sub> and C<sub>4</sub>, each of 12 μF, are connected so that C<sub>1</sub>, C<sub>2</sub> and C<sub>3</sub> are in series and this chain is in parallel with C<sub>4</sub>. The network is connected across a 500 V supply. Find the equivalent capacitance of the network and the charge on each capacitor.
pyq.answer:
Series chain: 1/C' = 3/12, C' = 4 μF. Parallel with C4: Ceq = 4 + 12 = 16 μF.

The chain and C4 both have 500 V across them. Charge on the chain = C'V = 4 × 10−6 × 500 = 2 × 10−3 C, and this is the charge on each of C1, C2, C3 (series capacitors carry equal charge).

Charge on C4 = 12 × 10−6 × 500 = 6 × 10−3 C. Total charge drawn = 8 × 10−3 C = CeqV, as a check.

pyq.q: Find the ratio of the potential differences that must be applied across the parallel and series combination of two capacitors C<sub>1</sub> and C<sub>2</sub> with their capacitances in the ratio 1 : 2 so that the energy stored in the two cases becomes the same.
pyq.answer:
Let C1 = C, C2 = 2C. Parallel: Cp = 3C. Series: Cs = C × 2C/(C + 2C) = 2C/3.

Equal energies: ½CpVp2 = ½CsVs2 → Vp2/Vs2 = Cs/Cp = (2C/3)/3C = 2/9.

Vp : Vs = √2 : 3.

pyq.q: Two identical parallel plate capacitors A and B are connected in parallel to a battery of V volts. The battery is then disconnected and the space between the plates of capacitor B is filled with a dielectric of constant K. Find the ratio of the total electrostatic energy stored in both capacitors before and after the introduction of the dielectric.
pyq.answer:
Before: each has charge CV and energy ½CV2; total U1 = CV2.

After the battery is removed the total charge 2CV is fixed. A has capacitance C, B has KC, and they are still in parallel, so the common potential is V' = 2CV/(C + KC) = 2V/(1 + K).

U2 = ½(C + KC)V'2 = ½C(1 + K) × 4V2/(1 + K)2 = 2CV2/(1 + K).

U1 : U2 = CV2 : 2CV2/(1 + K) = (1 + K) : 2.

pyq.q: Two point charges q and −2q are kept a distance d apart. Find the location of the point relative to charge q at which the potential due to this system of charges is zero.
pyq.answer:
Let the point be at distance x from q on the line joining them.

Between the charges: q/x = 2q/(d − x) → d − x = 2x → x = d/3.

On the far side of q (away from −2q): q/x = 2q/(d + x) → d + x = 2x → x = d.

So the potential is zero at d/3 from q between the charges and at a distance d from q on the side away from −2q. No zero exists beyond −2q, because there the larger charge is always closer.

pyq.q: (a) Derive an expression for the electric potential at a point due to an electric dipole at a general point (r, θ). Hence obtain the potential on the axial line and on the equatorial line. (b) Depict the equipotential surfaces due to an electric dipole.
pyq.answer:
(a) Dipole: −q at A and +q at B, AB = 2a, centre O, p = 2qa from −q to +q. Point P at OP = r, angle θ with the axis; r1 = BP (from +q), r2 = AP (from −q).

V = (q/4πε0)(1/r1 − 1/r2).

r12 = r2 + a2 − 2ar cos θ; r22 = r2 + a2 + 2ar cos θ.

For r ≫ a, neglect a2/r2: r1 ≈ r(1 − 2a cos θ/r)½, so 1/r1 ≈ (1/r)(1 + a cos θ/r); similarly 1/r2 ≈ (1/r)(1 − a cos θ/r).

1/r1 − 1/r2 ≈ 2a cos θ/r2.

V = (q/4πε0) × 2a cos θ/r2 = (1/4πε0) p cos θ/r2 = (1/4πε0) p·r̂/r2.

Axial line: θ = 0°, V = p/(4πε0r2) (positive on the side of +q; negative for θ = 180°). Equatorial line: θ = 90°, V = 0.

(b) Draw closed surfaces around +q (positive potentials) and around −q (negative potentials), with the equatorial plane as the flat zero-potential surface between them; field lines cross every surface at right angles.

pyq.q: (a) Obtain the expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with a dielectric slab of thickness t (t < d) between the plates of separation d. (b) A slab of material of dielectric constant K has the same area as the plates of a parallel plate capacitor but thickness 3d/4, where d is the plate separation. Find the ratio of the capacitance with the slab to that without it.
pyq.answer:
(a) Plates of area A carry ±σ = ±Q/A. The field in the air part of the gap is E0 = σ/ε0. Inside the dielectric the induced surface charges −σp and +σp reduce the field to E = E0/K.

The potential difference is the sum over the two regions: V = E0(d − t) + (E0/K)t = (σ/ε0)(d − t + t/K) = (Q/ε0A)(d − t + t/K).

C = Q/V = ε0A/(d − t + t/K).

Checks: t = 0 gives ε0A/d; t = d gives Kε0A/d.

(b) With t = 3d/4: C = ε0A/(d − 3d/4 + 3d/4K) = ε0A/[(d/4)(1 + 3/K)] = 4Kε0A/[d(K + 3)].

C/C0 = [4Kε0A/d(K + 3)]/(ε0A/d) = 4K/(K + 3).

pyq.q: (a) State the expression for the energy stored in a charged parallel plate capacitor (the current CBSE syllabus asks for the formula only, not its derivation) and use it to obtain the expression for the energy density of the electric field. (b) A 12 pF capacitor is charged to 50 V and then disconnected. It is connected to an uncharged 6 pF capacitor. Find the common potential and the energy lost.
pyq.answer:
(a) The energy stored in a charged capacitor is U = Q2/2C = ½CV2 = ½QV (only the formula is required; the current CBSE syllabus does not ask for its derivation, so it is not reproduced here — the steps are given in the section body above for reference).

To get the energy density, apply this formula to a parallel plate capacitor: C = ε0A/d and V = Ed, so U = ½CV2 = ½(ε0A/d)E2d2 = ½ε0E2(Ad). The volume between the plates is Ad, so the energy density u = U/Ad = ½ε0E2.

(b) Q = 12 × 10−12 × 50 = 6 × 10−10 C. Common potential V = Q/(C1 + C2) = 6 × 10−10/18 × 10−12 = 33.3 V.

U1 = ½ × 12 × 10−12 × 2500 = 1.5 × 10−8 J. U2 = ½ × 18 × 10−12 × (33.3)2 = 1.0 × 10−8 J.

Energy lost = 0.5 × 10−8 J = 5 × 10−9 J. Check by formula: C1C2V12/2(C1 + C2) = 12 × 6 × 10−24 × 2500/(2 × 18 × 10−12) = 5 × 10−9 J.

pyq.q: (a) Obtain the expression for the potential energy of a system of two point charges q<sub>1</sub> and q<sub>2</sub> placed at r<sub>1</sub> and r<sub>2</sub> in an external electric field. (b) A parallel plate capacitor is charged by a battery, and a dielectric slab of constant K is then inserted while the battery remains connected. How do (i) the charge, (ii) the electric field between the plates, (iii) the capacitance and (iv) the energy stored change?
pyq.answer:
(a) Let the external potential be V(r). Bring q1 from infinity to r1: work W1 = q1V(r1) (no other charge is present yet).

Bring q2 to r2: it does work against the external field, q2V(r2), and against the field of q1, q1q2/(4πε0r12), where r12 = |r1 − r2|.

U = W1 + W2 = q1V(r1) + q2V(r2) + q1q2/(4πε0r12).

(b) The battery keeps V fixed. (i) Charge: C becomes KC, so Q = CV becomes KQ, increases K times (the battery supplies the extra charge). (ii) Field: E = V/d, unchanged. (iii) Capacitance: increases to KC. (iv) Energy: U = ½CV2 increases to KU.

pyq.q:
A dielectric is an insulating material with no free charges. When placed in an electric field its molecules are polarised: non-polar molecules acquire an induced dipole moment, and the permanent dipoles of polar molecules align partly with the field. The result is a layer of induced charge on each face of the dielectric, producing a field opposite to the applied one, so the net field inside the dielectric is reduced by the factor K, the dielectric constant. Filling a capacitor with a dielectric therefore raises its capacitance K times. Every dielectric also has a dielectric strength, the largest field it can bear without breaking down.
(i) Name one polar and one non-polar molecule.
(ii) A capacitor of 8 pF with air between its plates is filled completely with a dielectric of K = 5. What is the new capacitance?
(iii) If the capacitor in (ii) was charged to 100 V and then disconnected before the dielectric was inserted, what is the new potential difference?
(iv) Why does a dielectric only reduce, and not cancel, the field inside it, unlike a conductor?
pyq.answer:
(i) Polar: H2O or HCl. Non-polar: H2, O2, N2 or CO2.

(ii) C' = KC = 5 × 8 = 40 pF.

(iii) The charge is fixed at Q = CV = 8 pF × 100 V = 800 pC. V' = Q/C' = 800/40 = 20 V (that is, V/K).

(iv) A dielectric has only bound charges, which can be displaced slightly but not moved freely. The induced surface charge is less than the free charge on the plates (σp < σ), so the field is reduced to E0/K but not to zero. In a conductor free electrons move until the induced charge exactly cancels the applied field inside.

pyq.q:
An equipotential surface is one on which the electrostatic potential is the same at every point. For a single point charge the surfaces are concentric spheres; for a uniform field they are parallel planes perpendicular to the field. The electric field is always normal to an equipotential surface, and it is related to the potential by E = −dV/dr, so the field points in the direction in which the potential decreases fastest. Where the surfaces are crowded the field is strong; where they are far apart the field is weak.
(i) How much work is done in moving a charge of 5 μC between two points on an equipotential surface?
(ii) Two equipotential surfaces at 20 V and 10 V are 2 cm apart in a uniform field. Find the magnitude of the field and state its direction.
(iii) Why are the equipotential spheres around a point charge not equally spaced for equal steps of potential?
(iv) Can two equipotential surfaces of different potential intersect? Why?
pyq.answer:
(i) Zero; the potential difference between the points is zero, so W = qΔV = 0.

(ii) E = −ΔV/Δr in magnitude = (20 − 10)/0.02 = 500 V m−1, directed from the 20 V surface towards the 10 V surface (from higher to lower potential), normal to the surfaces.

(iii) V = q/(4πε0r) changes rapidly near the charge and slowly far away. Equal steps of V therefore need small steps of r near the charge and large ones far from it, so the spheres spread out with distance.

(iv) No. At the point of intersection the potential would have two values at once, and the field, being normal to both surfaces, would have two directions, which is impossible.

common_mistakes: Reporting the potential of a negative charge as a magnitude. Unlike the field formula, V = q/(4πε<sub>0</sub>r) carries the sign of q; a negative potential is the answer, and the examiner deducts for dropping the sign.
Adding potentials with cos θ components as if they were vectors. Potential is a scalar: add the signed values and nothing else.

Mixing up which quantity is fixed when a dielectric is inserted. Battery connected means V fixed and Q rises; battery removed means Q fixed and V falls. Writing 'charge increases' in the disconnected case loses the whole part.

Using the resistor rules for capacitors. Series capacitors follow the reciprocal rule and parallel capacitors add; the reverse gives a wrong equivalent capacitance and every charge computed from it is wrong.

Forgetting that series capacitors carry the same charge, and instead splitting the charge among them. In a network, the charge on a series chain is C<sub>chain</sub> times the voltage across the chain, and every member holds that full charge.
Counting only adjacent pairs in the potential energy of four charges at the corners of a square. There are six pairs, and the diagonal separation is √2 times the side.
Writing the dipole potential energy as U = pE cos θ or leaving out the statement that the zero is taken at θ = 90°. The sign and the reference position are both marking points.
Saying 'energy is not conserved' when two capacitors are connected. Charge is conserved; the lost energy goes into heat and radiation in the connecting wires, and the answer should say so.
strategy:
Split the chapter into two halves and give each two evenings. The first half is potential: learn the point-charge derivation, the dipole derivation with its two approximations, the potential energy of a system of charges, and the dipole in an external field with U = −pE cos θ. Write each derivation out once without the book and compare line by line with NCERT; the marking scheme follows NCERT's steps. Then practise the standard sketches: equipotential surfaces for a point charge, a uniform field, a dipole and two like charges, and the E and V graphs against r. These are 2-mark questions you can bank.

The second half is capacitors. Derive C = ε0A/d from Gauss's law, then the dielectric versions (fully filled and slab t < d), then series and parallel, then the energy-density derivation u = ½ε0E2 (U = Q2/2C itself is formula-only in the current CBSE syllabus — know it, but you will not be asked to derive it). Make a two-column table of what happens to Q, V, E, C and U with the battery connected and with it removed; it answers a family of questions on its own.

Then solve every NCERT exercise 2.1 to 2.11 and the board favourites in this guide: the unknown-C-and-V problem, the four-capacitor network, energy sharing between two capacitors, and the dipole torque-to-energy numerical. Recompute each answer with the other energy formula as a check. On the day, the 5-mark question from Unit I is usually a derivation plus a small numerical; write the derivation with the diagram and every named step, and leave the numerical for last so the derivation is complete.
